analysis.one_liner: Bans mining and energy development on federal lands in Montana's North Fork watershed.
analysis.headline: Passed the House by voice vote on March 4, 2014, then sat on the Senate calendar for the rest of the Congress and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently take federal land in the North Fork watershed of northwestern Montana off the table for mining claims, and, under the later House-passed version, for mineral and energy leasing. The idea is to protect the streams that feed the Flathead River system from the pollution and disturbance that hardrock mining and drilling bring. The House passed it quickly and without controversy — a voice vote, meaning no recorded roll call. But after the House passed it on March 4, 2014, the bill was placed on the Senate's calendar of bills waiting for floor time and the Senate never took it up before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Montana residents and downstream water users, people who fish, float, and hunt the North Fork drainage, the gateway towns and tourism economy around Glacier National Park, and anyone who drinks water downstream of the Flathead headwaters. Watershed protection keeps hardrock mine waste and drilling activity out of the headwaters of a major river system.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Montana residents, recreation economy, water users

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws federally owned land and land interests in the North Fork Lands Withdrawal Area of Montana from all forms of location, entry, and patent under the mining laws, meaning no new mining claims can be staked there.
The withdrawal covers the whole North Fork watershed area in Montana, protecting rivers, lakes, and streams in that drainage from new mineral development.
The House approved the bill without recorded opposition, passing it by voice vote under a fast-track procedure that is used for noncontroversial bills.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies and oil, gas, and geothermal developers that would have been able to stake claims or lease federal land in the North Fork area. Also, in a modest way, the federal treasury and local economies, which forgo any mineral revenue and jobs the land might have produced — a cost bill supporters judged small against the value of protecting the watershed.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently forecloses mineral development on a large block of federal land. Miners and energy developers lost access to whatever deposits the North Fork area holds, along with the royalties and jobs that development could have brought to northwestern Montana.

A good-faith objection is that a blanket withdrawal locks up federal resources without a case-by-case review; a project that could be built safely would be barred along with a bad one, and the land cannot be revisited if mining technology improves or prices change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — permanent protection of a scenic headwaters watershed from mine waste and drilling — is broad and permanent, while the cost is forgone mineral development whose value was speculative. That trade is why the House passed it by voice vote with a Republican sponsor from Montana. The bill's real failure was procedural, not substantive: the Senate never voted on a measure its House had approved with no recorded opposition.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote in March 2014, but it sat on the Senate's waiting calendar until the Congress ended without the Senate ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Introduced June 5, 2013 by Rep. Steve Daines of Montana and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, including its public lands and energy subcommittees.
The committee marked the bill up on January 28, 2014 and reported it to the House with an amendment on February 28, 2014.
On March 4, 2014 the House passed the amended bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure reserved for noncontroversial measures.

The bill was then placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — the queue of bills cleared to receive floor time — but the Senate never called it up for a vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining and oil, gas, and geothermal interests did best from the outcome: the House-passed withdrawal never became law through this bill, so the North Fork federal lands stayed open to mineral claims and leasing activity under existing law.

for.name: Rep. Steve Daines (R-MT)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it through House passage by voice vote in March 2014.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-NV)
against.what_they_did: Controlled which bills received Senate floor time; H.R. 2259 sat on the Senate's waiting calendar from March 2014 until the Congress ended without ever being scheduled for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor from Montana, passed the House by voice vote with no recorded roll call, and died without any recorded Senate vote, so no party split shows up anywhere in the record.

industries.note: The bill bars new mining claims on federal land across the North Fork watershed, permanently closing an area to prospecting and mine development. Mining's interest in keeping the land open ran against the water-quality and recreation interests of residents.
Federal land in the area would be unavailable for energy leasing, foreclosing drilling activity in the watershed. Industry's interest ran against watershed protection.

The North Fork drainage borders Glacier National Park country; keeping mining and drilling out of the headwaters protects the scenery, fisheries, and river quality that recreation businesses depend on. Its interest ran alongside residents' interest in clean water.
